prompt: Strathern's phrasing of Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a ___, it ceases to be a good measure.
What does the lesson say Goodhart's and Campbell's laws describe?

choices.text: Dishonest people falsifying their figures
choices.why: Nobody has to lie for the laws to hold.

choices.text: A mistake that only happens in economics
choices.why: Campbell wrote about social indicators; delivery metrics are exposed too.

choices.text: What honest people do with a number they are rewarded for
choices.why: Right. They find the cheapest way to move it, and each step is defensible.

choices.text: Measurements that are too imprecise to use
choices.why: The measure can be precise and still bend once it is a target.

prompt: Why does a team that uses its own cycle time to find its own bottleneck have no reason to game it?

choices.text: Gaming would only blind the team to its own problem
choices.why: Right. Nobody gains from fooling the instrument they steer by.

choices.text: Cycle time is impossible to manipulate
choices.why: Splitting cards and moving work off the board manipulate it easily.

choices.text: Teams that measure themselves are more honest people
choices.why: The difference is the use of the number, not the people.

choices.text: Nobody outside the team can see it
choices.why: Visibility is fine; what matters is that nobody is rewarded by it.

prompt: Match each trick to the metric it inflates.

pairs.left: deploying each service separately at the same minute
measuring from the merge after squashing a week's work
fixing forward quietly instead of recording a rollback
starting the clock at the incident declaration

prompt: Why does every trick that inflates deployment frequency also flatter the change failure rate?

choices.text: Because more deployments catch more bugs
choices.why: Counted deployments catch nothing; they are the same runs.

choices.text: Because failures are only counted weekly
choices.why: Nothing about the counting period changed.

choices.text: Because the pipeline runs faster
choices.why: The pipeline is untouched by a counting trick.

choices.text: The rate divides by deployments
choices.why: Right. A bigger denominator with the same failures is a smaller rate.

prompt: An item at forty days old is split into two new items. Which chart improves, and what changed for the work?

choices.text: The CFD improves, because two items finish instead of one
choices.why: Neither has finished; the board just has a new card.

choices.text: The ageing chart looks fresh; the work did not move
choices.why: Right. Splitting can be good practice, but done to reset age it only changes what is counted.

choices.text: Lead time for changes improves
choices.why: That metric is not about cards at all.

choices.text: Nothing changes on any chart
choices.why: The oldest dot disappears from the ageing chart.

prompt: What do all the tricks in the catalogue have in common?

choices.text: They change what is counted, not what happens to the work
choices.why: Right. The general test: if the number moved, ask which events changed.

choices.text: They all require changing the pipeline
choices.why: Most need no change at all, only a new way of counting.

choices.text: They are all forbidden by the DORA research
choices.why: The research forbids nothing; it measures.

choices.text: They only work on teams that deploy daily
choices.why: They work at any frequency.

prompt: game.py counts 72 deployments in 61 days when each change is counted separately. How many deployments per week is that, to one decimal place?
In game.py's one-per-change line, which numbers stayed exactly the same as recorded?

choices.text: Deployment frequency and the failure rate
choices.why: Those are the two that moved.

choices.text: The failure count and deployment frequency
choices.why: The failure count stayed; the frequency nearly doubled.

choices.text: Lead time for changes and time to restore
choices.why: Right. They are measured on changes and failures, which the trick cannot touch.

choices.text: None of them
choices.why: Two stayed put, which is the trick's signature.

prompt: A report shows a change failure rate of 0% and a dash where the time to restore used to be. What is the likeliest reading?

choices.text: The team has become perfect
choices.why: Possible, and less likely than a moved definition.

choices.text: The pipeline stopped recording restores
choices.why: The dash is what no failures leaves behind, whatever the cause.

choices.text: Time to restore is no longer a DORA metric
choices.why: It still is, under its 2023 name.

choices.text: Failure was redefined so nothing counts
choices.why: Right. Zero failures leave nothing to measure; check the definition log.

prompt: Under the rule that only failures taking more than 60 minutes count, how many of the Billing team's two August and September failures, restored in 48 and 55 minutes, still count?
Which signs gave the two tricks away? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Metrics the trick could not reach stayed flat
choices.why: Right. Lead time and restore did not move.

choices.text: A number became undefined
choices.why: Right. The dash for time to restore.

choices.text: More deployments than pipeline runs
choices.why: Right. 72 from 38 runs matches no event.

choices.text: The failures happened on different days
choices.why: They were on the same days in every version.

prompt: How do you tell batches made smaller by real flow from batches made smaller by counting?

choices.text: Real batches always produce more deployments
choices.why: Both produce more counted deployments; that is the disguise.

choices.text: Real ones also cut lead time and time to restore
choices.why: Right. Those are measured on changes and failures, which counting cannot fake.

choices.text: Real ones lower the failure rate and fake ones raise it
choices.why: The fake one lowered it too, from 5% to 3%.

choices.text: Only an audit by another team can tell
choices.why: The data itself tells, in four questions.

prompt: A team truly deploys every change on its own, with its own pipeline run, and its requesters still wait a month. What is going on?

choices.text: It is gaming its metrics
choices.why: Nothing here is fake; every deployment is real.

choices.text: Its pipeline must be broken
choices.why: The pipeline is the part that works.

choices.text: Its delay is somewhere the four metrics do not see
choices.why: Right. A review queue or a backlog; check the customer's lead time.

choices.text: Small batches never help
choices.why: They help; they just cannot fix a wait that is upstream of them.

prompt: Put the chain by which the Billing team's batches really got smaller in order.
What should happen to every change of a metric's definition?

choices.text: It should be avoided at all costs
choices.why: Most changes are reasonable; they need to be visible, not forbidden.

choices.text: It should be applied backwards to all history silently
choices.why: Silence is exactly the danger.

choices.text: It should be approved by the DORA team
choices.why: Nobody outside the team owns its definitions.

choices.text: It goes in a dated log
choices.why: Right. A step on a chart can then be checked against the log in a minute.

prompt: Match each metric to the one the lesson says to watch beside it.

pairs.right: change failure rate and pipeline runs
items split or moved off the board

prompt: Why does the lesson say to show counts beside every rate?

choices.text: A rate hides its numerator and denominator
choices.why: Right. 3% could be 2 of 72 or 1 of 38, and only the counts show a jump in either.

choices.text: Because rates cannot be computed for small teams
choices.why: They can; they are fragile, which counts reveal.

choices.text: Because stakeholders prefer large numbers
choices.why: Preference is not the reason.

choices.text: Because DORA reports always show counts
choices.why: The reason is detection, not imitation.

prompt: You find that a developer split deployments to improve the team's frequency before a quarterly review. What does the lesson say to do first?

choices.text: Raise it as misconduct with their manager
choices.why: That teaches everybody to hide the next trick better.

choices.text: Recompute the numbers and say nothing
choices.why: Silence leaves the incentive in place.

choices.text: Fix the incentive that made the trick worth doing
choices.why: Right. Change the question, write the definition down, and the trick stops paying.

choices.text: Ban deployments of single changes
choices.why: Single-change deployments can be good practice; counting is the problem.

prompt: Deployment frequency doubled this month and the number of pipeline runs did not change. What should you conclude?

choices.text: The team is twice as productive
choices.why: Nothing reached users any differently.

choices.text: The counting changed, not the delivery
choices.why: Right. More deployments from the same runs match no event.

choices.text: The pipeline is now faster
choices.why: Faster runs would not multiply the count.

choices.text: The failure rate must have risen
choices.why: It would have fallen, with a bigger denominator.

prompt: A team had 3 failures in 30 deployments. After counting each service separately it reports 90 deployments with the same 3 failures. What is the new failure rate, as a whole percentage?
Under which use of a number does the lesson say Goodhart's law bites hardest?

choices.text: When pay, rating or standing depends on it
choices.why: Right. Then the number starts answering how we look, not how we work.

choices.text: When the team reads it every morning
choices.why: Frequent reading by the team that owns it is the healthy use.

choices.text: When it is drawn as a chart rather than a table
choices.why: The form of display is not the issue.

choices.text: When it is computed by a program
choices.why: Programs compute what they are told; the incentive is human.
